Issued at 220 PM CDT Fri Sep 18 2026

Rest of Today - Saturday Morning: Widespread Rain, Heavy Rain 
Leading to Flooding Concerns Overnight 

Rainfall has spread into portions of the region as stratiform 
rainfall from the deepening surface low we have advertised over the 
last couple of days is pushing eastward. With some dry air 
intrusion through portions of Iowa, have noticed a lull in 
precipitation generally near and south of I-90 this afternoon, 
which much of the CAMs suggest will persist into the early 
evening. The key mechanism we are watching for which will come 
later this evening and into the overnight is a fairly profound 
surge of 850mb moisture transport as the nocturnal low-level jet
enhances and interacts with a quasi-stationary boundary 
situated over the region. As this occurs, the recent RAP 
generally agrees on advecting some more favorable MUCAPE into 
the region which in turn switches precipitation mode from 
stratiform to convective as illustrated uniformly across all of 
the CAMs. Consequently, heavy rain and flooding concerns begin 
to increase across much of the area during the overnight as 
precipitable waters approaching 2 inches and warm cloud depths 
over 4km would suggest a substantially primed environment for 
heavy rainfall with fairly strong sloping frontogenesis where 
the instability can reside atop this. In addition, the moisture 
transport vector may eventually turn more westerly which may 
aid in allowing for some backbuilding convection overnight and 
into the early morning hours, however the CAMs disagree to what
extent this occurs as the stronger 0-3km shear vector present 
in the RAP would suggest some MCS organization which could keep 
convection more progressive. 

As far as amounts are concerned, the inter-quartile range in the NBM 
for rainfall amounts over generally ranges between 1-3" across much 
of the region. When looking at the 90th percentile to ensemble 
maximum of the NBM, some pockets of 4-6"+ begin to show up. As a 
result, would think that the general story with this event will be a 
widespread 1-3" of rainfall but localized higher amounts where 
storms manage to traverse the same locations. Consequently, have 
expanded the Flood Watch to encompass the area where these higher 
amounts may be possible. If a more northern solution does take place 
with this system, portions of northeast IA may underachieve for
rainfall amounts overnight with a few members in the lower 
percentiles of the NBM having amounts under 1". For hydrological
impacts across the region in light of this rainfall, refer to 
the hydro section for additional details. 

Aside from the rainfall impacts, cannot fully rule (under 10% 
chance) out some stronger storms overnight as well as the 
aforementioned instability pushes into the region. In general, shear 
profiles in RAP hodographs are not overly impressive, however modest 
mid-level lapse rates of around 6-6.5 C/km and MUCAPE values 
approaching 2000 J/kg may allow for some small hail or gusty winds 
with any descending cores, granted the heavy precipitation 
environment here would likely limit hail size substantially. In
any case, storms will likely exit the region by early Saturday 
morning with the heavy rain and strong storm threat quickly 
diminishing after sunrise. 

Saturday - Monday: Cooler, Additional Heavy Rain Possible 
Saturday Afternoon/Evening in Southwest WI and Northeast IA

After we get past this system, continued rain chances remain across 
portions of the area as an upper-level trough/low slowly pivots 
through the Great Plains with the aforementioned boundary still in 
place. Consequently, additional periods of rainfall remain possible 
through Monday with zonal flow in place with some 850mb moisture 
transport running overtop this. The most reasonable shot for 
additional rainfall would likely be Saturday afternoon and into the 
evening for portions of southwest Wisconsin as a more profound axis 
of 850mb moisture transport pushes north into southwest Wisconsin as 
shown in the NAM/GFS. Will need to watch this as convective 
initiation with this forcing begins to develop in far southwest 
Wisconsin and northeast Iowa by afternoon which could lead to 
additional heavy rainfall. Overall, confidence is low in how 
this would manifest, but some of the CAMs suggest some pockets 
of additional amounts of around 1-2" could be possible where 
storms form which could certainly result in flooding issues 
considering tonight's rainfall. 

Otherwise, the quasi-stationary boundary responsible for all of
this will gradually sag south into Sunday and Monday so would 
expect precipitation potential to gradually diminish into 
Monday. The NBM suggests some uptick in precipitation 
probabilities into Monday as the aforementioned main upper-level
trough/low pivots over the area on Monday. However,
